7	## Signature
8	- G (zone-centre E2g) near 1580 cm-1 and 2D (second order of zone-boundary TO phonons) near 2700 cm-1 at
9	  514 nm; D near 1350 cm-1 needs a defect or edge; 1L 2D is a single sharp peak about 4x higher than G; 1L G
10	  sits 3 to 5 cm-1 above bulk graphite (Ferrari et al. 2006, PRL 97, 187401; arXiv cond-mat/0606284, p.2).
11	  [consensus]
12	- D' near 1620 cm-1, D+D', 2D' and D+D'' are further double-resonance bands; 2D is present without defects
13	  (Ferrari and Basko 2013, Nat. Nanotechnol. 8, 235; arXiv 1306.5856, Fig. 1g, pp.3-6).
14	- Peak areas are more robust than heights: perturbations that only change phonon lifetimes conserve area
15	  (Ferrari and Basko 2013, p.14). State whether a ratio is I (height) or A (area).
16	
17	## Thickness and stacking
18	- 2L Bernal: 2D broader, upshifted, four components; up to 5 layers the 2D shape still changes; above 5
19	  layers hardly distinguishable from graphite (Ferrari 2006, p.2, Fig. 2b,c). [consensus]
20	- A single-Lorentzian 2D is not proof of 1L: turbostratic graphite also has one 2D peak, about twice as wide
21	  and upshifted about 20 cm-1, often with a D peak (Ferrari and Basko 2013, p.9). Grown (CVD) films need this
22	  check. [consensus]
23	- Twisted bilayer (Kim et al. 2012, PRL 108, 246103; arXiv 1201.4221, pp.4-6, Figs. 2-3; 633 nm): below about
24	  8 deg strong-coupling spectra; above about 13 deg close to 1L. G intensity rises more than thirty-fold near
25	  10 to 11 deg at 633 nm; the resonance angle grows with laser energy (about 13 deg at 514 nm). 2D blueshift vs
26	  1L is non-monotonic (up to 22 cm-1 at 10 deg). Below 10 deg the 2D area is about half that of two decoupled
27	  layers.
28	- Twist also activates non-dispersive superlattice peaks (one in 1350 to 1550 cm-1, one near 1620 cm-1;
29	  Ferrari and Basko 2013, p.9) named R and R' in later work. A huge G with weak 2D at one laser line means
30	  "check twist resonance", not "thick flake".
31	- Bernal (ABA) vs rhombohedral (ABC) trilayer: distinct 2D line shapes; ABA has a higher intensity-weighted mean
32	  2D shift than ABC with similar dispersion (Lui et al. 2011, Nano Lett. 11, 164; arXiv 1011.3021, SI p.9).
33	  Thicker stacks have intermediate stackings; far-field imaging can miss sub-micron domains (Lu et al. 2025,
34	  Nature 637; doi 10.1038/s41586-024-08470-1, p.7, via Lit-RAG).
35	- Shear (C) mode near 31 cm-1 in 2L scales with N but lies below many notch/edge filters; absence of C is not
36	  evidence of 1L (Ferrari and Basko 2013, p.2). LO+ZO' combination near 1700 to 1750 cm-1 also tracks N.
37	
38	## Strain and doping
39	- Uniaxial strain splits G into G+ and G- (-10.8 and -31.7 cm-1/%), 2D -64 cm-1/% (Mohiuddin 2009 via Ferrari
40	  and Basko 2013, p.20, Eq. S10). Biaxial strain shifts without splitting (same, p.20). [consensus]
41	- G stiffens and narrows for both electron and hole doping (non-adiabatic Kohn anomaly); 2D rises for holes and
42	  softens only at high electron doping; I(2D)/I(G) falls strongly with doping (Das et al. 2008, Nat.
43	  Nanotechnol. 3, 210; arXiv 0709.1174, abstract and pp.4-5). [consensus]
44	- Separate strain and doping by the (Pos G, Pos 2D) vector plot: strain line slope 2.2 +- 0.2 (Lee et al. 2012,
45	  Nat. Commun. 3, 1024; arXiv 1209.0234, p.3, Fig. 2). Model assumptions (514.5 nm origin, hole doping) limit
46	  transfer to other lasers or electron doping. [disputed in detail, widely used]
47	- Very high doping suppresses 2D when 2|E_F| exceeds the scattered photon energy (Ferrari and Basko 2013,
48	  pp.18-19, Fig. S3). Annealing on SiO2 raises G and 2D by about 25 cm-1 (hole doping) (Lee 2012, p.3).
49	
50	## Defects and quality
51	- Stage 1 (L_D above about 3 nm): D and D' appear and grow, peaks broaden; stage 2: Pos(G) falls towards 1510,
52	  I(D)/I(G) drops, second order becomes a bump (Ferrari and Basko 2013, p.10). I(D)/I(G) peaks near L_D 3 nm,
53	  so one ratio gives two densities; FWHM(G) decides: about 14 cm-1 through stage 1, much larger in stage 2
54	  (Cancado et al. 2011, Nano Lett. 11, 3190; arXiv 1105.0175, p.5, Fig. 5c). [consensus]
55	- Defect type from I(D)/I(D') in stage 1: about 13 sp3, about 7 vacancy, about 3.5 boundaries (Eckmann et al.
56	  2012, Nano Lett. 12, 3925; arXiv 1207.2058, abstract, p.6). Only valid in stage 1. [one group, often reproduced]
57	- Doping lowers D and D' intensity at fixed defect count; ignoring E_F about 0.5 eV underestimated n_D by more
58	  than 2x in their example (Bruna et al. 2014, ACS Nano; arXiv 1405.4264, p.5). Check doping before L_D.
59	- Raman-silent defects: perfect zigzag edges, charged impurities, intercalants, strain give no D peak (Ferrari
60	  and Basko 2013, p.11). No D peak does not mean defect-free in every sense.
61	- Edges: D only from armchair-like segments; I(D) proportional to cos^2 theta (cos^4 with parallel analyzer)
62	  to the edge; I(D)min/I(D)max measures edge disorder (Ferrari and Basko 2013, p.8). A D peak confined to
63	  edges in a map is an edge effect, not bulk damage.
64	- Sub-spot strain variations broaden 2D: hBN-encapsulated FWHM(2D) mostly 16 to 20 cm-1 vs above 22 cm-1 on
65	  SiO2 (Neumann et al. 2015, Nat. Commun. 6, 8429; arXiv 1406.7771, p.2, Fig. 1h). FWHM(2D) is a flatness and
66	  quality metric.
67	
68	## Temperature and heating
69	- Supported 1L: G -0.016, 2D -0.034 cm-1/K, 83 to 373 K (Calizo et al. 2007; arXiv 0708.1223, Table I p.7).
70	  Suspended 1L: 2D -0.072, G -0.044 cm-1/K (Chen et al., relayed by Lee et al. 2011, PRB 83, 081419; arXiv
71	  1103.3337, p.2). The difference is substrate thermal-expansion strain: coefficients do not transfer
72	  between supported and suspended samples. [consensus on the cause]
73	- Stokes/anti-Stokes thermometry is biased in graphene because incident and scattered resonance windows differ
74	  (Ferrari and Basko 2013, p.12).
75	
76	## Excitation wavelength
77	- D disperses about 52 and 2D about 2x that (about 100) cm-1/eV; G does not disperse in stage 1, about 6
78	  cm-1/eV in stage 2 (Cancado 2011, p.5; Ferrari and Basko 2013, p.7). Never compare D or 2D positions across
79	  lasers. I(D)/I(G) scales with lambda^4 (Cancado 2011).
80	- Twist resonances and doping-blocked 2D are laser-energy specific (Kim 2012; Ferrari and Basko 2013 Fig. S3).
81	
82	## Polarization and substrate
83	- I(2D)/I(G) changed by almost 370 % for a 60 % change in SiO2 thickness (Yoon et al. 2009, PRB 80, 125422;
84	  arXiv 0908.4322, abstract, Fig. 2). Substrate stack must be known before using intensity ratios.
85	- Strain-axis and edge-type determination use polarization (G+/G- and edge G selection rules; Ferrari and
86	  Basko 2013, pp.8, 19).
87	- In hBN-encapsulated samples the hBN E2g (about 1366 cm-1) overlaps D; D disperses with laser, hBN does not,
88	  so use a second wavelength (Purdie et al. 2018, Nat. Commun. 9, 5387; doi 10.1038/s41467-018-07558-3, p.6,
89	  via Lit-RAG).
90	
91	## Pitfalls and artifacts
92	- 2D at about 2700 cm-1 is outside many short-range acquisitions; a "missing 2D" may be range, not physics.
93	- Single Lorentzian 2D: test width and D peak before claiming 1L (turbostratic, twisted).
94	- G position alone cannot separate strain and doping; use the G-2D vector and FWHM(G).
95	- Defect quantification assumes stage 1, low doping, heights, and a known laser.
96	
97	## What to ask
98	- Laser wavelength and power at sample; substrate stack (SiO2 thickness), suspended or supported, encapsulation.
99	- Exfoliated or CVD or epitaxial; transfer and anneal history; gate or electrolyte; height or area ratios.
100	- Spectral resolution and calibration reference; mapped area and number of spectra.
101	
102	## Reference figures
103	- Ferrari 2006, arXiv cond-mat/0606284, Fig. 2: 2D shape vs layer number at 514 and 633 nm.
104	- Cancado 2011, arXiv 1105.0175, Figs. 3 and 5: I(D)/I(G) vs L_D for several lasers; FWHM(G) vs L_D.
105	- Lee 2012, arXiv 1209.0234, Fig. 2: Pos(G) vs Pos(2D) correlation, strain and doping axes.
106	- Kim 2012, arXiv 1201.4221, Figs. 2-3: G enhancement and 2D width and shift vs twist angle.

- Defect type from I(D)/I(D') in stage 1: about 13 sp3, about 7 vacancy, about 3.5 boundaries (Eckmann et al.
  2012, Nano Lett. 12, 3925; arXiv 1207.2058, abstract, p.6). Only valid in stage 1. [one group, often reproduced]
- Doping lowers D and D' intensity at fixed defect count; ignoring E_F about 0.5 eV underestimated n_D by more
  than 2x in their example (Bruna et al. 2014, ACS Nano; arXiv 1405.4264, p.5). Check doping before L_D.
- Raman-silent defects: perfect zigzag edges, charged impurities, intercalants, strain give no D peak (Ferrari
  and Basko 2013, p.11). No D peak does not mean defect-free in every sense.
- Edges: D only from armchair-like segments; I(D) proportional to cos^2 theta (cos^4 with parallel analyzer)
  to the edge; I(D)min/I(D)max measures edge disorder (Ferrari and Basko 2013, p.8). A D peak confined to
  edges in a map is an edge effect, not bulk damage.
- Sub-spot strain variations broaden 2D: hBN-encapsulated FWHM(2D) mostly 16 to 20 cm-1 vs above 22 cm-1 on
  SiO2 (Neumann et al. 2015, Nat. Commun. 6, 8429; arXiv 1406.7771, p.2, Fig. 1h). FWHM(2D) is a flatness and
  quality metric.

## Temperature and heating
- Supported 1L: G -0.016, 2D -0.034 cm-1/K, 83 to 373 K (Calizo et al. 2007; arXiv 0708.1223, Table I p.7).
  Suspended 1L: 2D -0.072, G -0.044 cm-1/K (Chen et al., relayed by Lee et al. 2011, PRB 83, 081419; arXiv
  1103.3337, p.2). The difference is substrate thermal-expansion strain: coefficients do not transfer
  between supported and suspended samples. [consensus on the cause]
- Stokes/anti-Stokes thermometry is biased in graphene because incident and scattered resonance windows differ
  (Ferrari and Basko 2013, p.12).

## Excitation wavelength
- D disperses about 52 and 2D about 2x that (about 100) cm-1/eV; G does not disperse in stage 1, about 6
  cm-1/eV in stage 2 (Cancado 2011, p.5; Ferrari and Basko 2013, p.7). Never compare D or 2D positions across
  lasers. I(D)/I(G) scales with lambda^4 (Cancado 2011).
- Twist resonances and doping-blocked 2D are laser-energy specific (Kim 2012; Ferrari and Basko 2013 Fig. S3).

## Polarization and substrate
- I(2D)/I(G) changed by almost 370 % for a 60 % change in SiO2 thickness (Yoon et al. 2009, PRB 80, 125422;
  arXiv 0908.4322, abstract, Fig. 2). Substrate stack must be known before using intensity ratios.
- Strain-axis and edge-type determination use polarization (G+/G- and edge G selection rules; Ferrari and
  Basko 2013, pp.8, 19).
- In hBN-encapsulated samples the hBN E2g (about 1366 cm-1) overlaps D; D disperses with laser, hBN does not,
  so use a second wavelength (Purdie et al. 2018, Nat. Commun. 9, 5387; doi 10.1038/s41467-018-07558-3, p.6,
  via Lit-RAG).

## Pitfalls and artifacts
- 2D at about 2700 cm-1 is outside many short-range acquisitions; a "missing 2D" may be range, not physics.
- Single Lorentzian 2D: test width and D peak before claiming 1L (turbostratic, twisted).
- G position alone cannot separate strain and doping; use the G-2D vector and FWHM(G).
- Defect quantification assumes stage 1, low doping, heights, and a known laser.

## What to ask
- Laser wavelength and power at sample; substrate stack (SiO2 thickness), suspended or supported, encapsulation.
- Exfoliated or CVD or epitaxial; transfer and anneal history; gate or electrolyte; height or area ratios.
- Spectral resolution and calibration reference; mapped area and number of spectra.

## Reference figures
- Ferrari 2006, arXiv cond-mat/0606284, Fig. 2: 2D shape vs layer number at 514 and 633 nm.
- Cancado 2011, arXiv 1105.0175, Figs. 3 and 5: I(D)/I(G) vs L_D for several lasers; FWHM(G) vs L_D.
- Lee 2012, arXiv 1209.0234, Fig. 2: Pos(G) vs Pos(2D) correlation, strain and doping axes.
- Kim 2012, arXiv 1201.4221, Figs. 2-3: G enhancement and 2D width and shift vs twist angle.

content.text:
**Summary.** The G and 2D differences are laser heating, not a change in strain or doping. The Si reference line stays within 0.05 cm⁻¹ across the three spectra. Use the 0.5 mW spectrum for any strain or doping analysis, and treat even that one as an upper bound on the unheated position. Do not use the 5 mW spectrum.

**What I measured** (after Si correction; fit errors only, so add about 0.2–0.3 cm⁻¹ for calibration):

| Power | G (cm⁻¹) | G FWHM | 2D (cm⁻¹) | 2D FWHM |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.5 mW | 1581.14 ± 0.10 | 13.4 ± 0.3 | 2669.32 ± 0.11 | 26.2 ± 0.4 |
| 2 mW | 1580.43 ± 0.08 | 14.5 ± 0.2 | 2666.23 ± 0.12 | 27.0 ± 0.4 |
| 5 mW | 1579.28 ± 0.06 | 15.6 ± 0.2 | 2664.17 ± 0.08 | 29.9 ± 0.3 |

- **Shifts, 0.5 to 5 mW:** G moves by −1.86 ± 0.12 cm⁻¹ and 2D by −5.15 ± 0.13 cm⁻¹. The shifts are monotonic, and both lines broaden: G by about 2.2 cm⁻¹ and 2D by about 3.7 cm⁻¹.
- **Calibration:** Si sits at 520.86, 520.90 and 520.91 cm⁻¹ (offsets +0.17 to +0.21 from 520.7). That is a scatter of 0.05 cm⁻¹, so calibration or drift cannot explain shifts of 2 to 5 cm⁻¹. Si does not shift downward, so the graphene is heated locally, not the whole chip.
- **Area per mW:** G area/power is 31.6k, 33.2k and 35.5k counts/mW, about 12% superlinear. The 2D/G height ratio is constant at 2.7 (0.366, 0.363 and 0.372 G/2D height). I take this as a mild change in coupling or focus, not a change in the sample.
- **D peak:** none is visible. The 1300–1400 cm⁻¹ region has no peak above the baseline in any spectrum. Defects are low.
- **Layer number:** 2D is a single Lorentzian of 26 cm⁻¹ FWHM. That is consistent with a monolayer on SiO₂ (Neumann 2015 gives >22 cm⁻¹ on SiO₂). It is not turbostratic, which would be about 50 cm⁻¹.

**Why this is heating**
- **Heating coefficients:** G and 2D soften together and broaden together. For supported monolayer graphene the coefficients are −0.016 cm⁻¹/K for G and −0.034 cm⁻¹/K for 2D (Calizo 2007, Table I). Applied to the shifts, the 0.5 to 5 mW change corresponds to about +115 K from G and about +150 K from 2D. These are consistent with each other within about 30%.
- **Doping:** this would move 2D by only about 0.7 times the G shift (Lee 2012, slope 0.70), and it narrows G (Das 2008). I observe Δ2D/ΔG = 2.8 ± 0.2 and a broadening G, so doping is excluded.
- **Strain:** the strain slope is 2.2 ± 0.2 (Lee 2012), so strain cannot be excluded on slope alone. But a 0.08% uniaxial strain would have to change reproducibly with laser power, and it would split G. No G splitting is seen. Strain from thermal-expansion mismatch with the substrate is just the same heating effect.
- **Unchanged ratios:** the 2D/G ratio and the G linewidth trend show no change in carrier density between powers.

**Strain and doping at 0.5 mW (low confidence)**
- **Reference:** Lee 2012 gives G = 1581.6 and 2D = 2676.9 cm⁻¹ as the strain-free, neutral origin at 514 nm. That relation is valid only at 513–516 nm.
- **Dispersion correction:** 2D disperses by about 100 cm⁻¹/eV (Ferrari and Basko 2013 and Cancado 2011). For 532 nm I estimate the origin near 2669 cm⁻¹, which is a rough ±3 cm⁻¹ correction.
- **Result:** G is within 0.5 cm⁻¹ of the origin, and 2D is close to it. The sample therefore looks near-neutral and nearly strain-free. FWHM(G) of 13.4 cm⁻¹ is also what you expect at low doping.
- **Limit:** I did not run the Lee decomposition, because 532 nm is outside its validity range. The conclusion is qualitative.

**What the data cannot tell**
- **Strain versus doping:** the G–2D vector method cannot be applied quantitatively at 532 nm. The heating drift is larger than any plausible static strain or doping signal.
- **Heating at 0.5 mW:** it is not zero. The 2D shift per mW is steeper between 0.5 and 2 mW (about −2.1 cm⁻¹/mW) than between 2 and 5 mW (about −0.7 cm⁻¹/mW), which is not a clean linear thermal response. The absolute temperature of the graphene is unknown.
- **Order of measurement:** the spectra were taken in the order 0.5, 2, 5 mW. Laser-induced desorption or annealing of dopants could have left permanent changes. I cannot rule this out without a repeat at 0.5 mW.
- **Weak band at 2318 cm⁻¹:** this appears only at 5 mW, with FWHM 33 ± 14 cm⁻¹ and position error ±4 cm⁻¹. It is marginal, and I did not interpret it.

**Questions for you**
- Was a 0.5 mW spectrum retaken after the 5 mW exposure? If it matches the first one, the changes were reversible and purely thermal.
- What is the SiO₂ thickness? It sets the 2D/G intensity ratio (Yoon 2009), and the observed 2.7 is below the textbook 4.
- Is the 0.5 mW figure the power at the sample, and what is the spot size?
- What are the exfoliation and anneal history and the environment (air or vacuum)? Annealing on SiO₂ changes doping (Lee 2012).

**Recommendation.** Repeat the measurement at 0.1 mW or lower, and take a power series. Extrapolate G and 2D to P → 0 and use those values as the cold position. A polarization-resolved or 514 nm measurement would let you apply the Lee decomposition properly.

structured_output.summary: The G and 2D differences are laser heating, not a change in strain or doping. G moves from 1581.14 to 1579.28 cm-1 (-1.86 ± 0.12) and 2D from 2669.32 to 2664.17 cm-1 (-5.15 ± 0.13) between 0.5 and 5 mW, and both lines broaden. Si is stable to 0.05 cm-1, so it is not calibration. The shifts match the supported-graphene temperature coefficients for a rise of about 115 to 150 K. Trust the 0.5 mW spectrum for strain and doping, as an upper bound on the cold position, and do not use the 5 mW one. At 0.5 mW the sample looks near-neutral, nearly strain-free, defect-free (no D peak) and monolayer-like, but this is qualitative at 532 nm.

observations.finding: G and 2D downshift and broaden with laser power; this is laser heating.
Calibration or drift is excluded as the cause of the shifts.
observations.evidence: Si line 520.86 / 520.90 / 520.91 cm-1 (offsets +0.17 to +0.21 from 520.7), a scatter of 0.05 cm-1 versus shifts of 2 to 5 cm-1. Si does not shift downward, so only the graphene is hot.

observations.finding: The shifts are consistent with a thermal rise of roughly 115 to 150 K between 0.5 and 5 mW.
observations.evidence: -1.86 cm-1 / -0.016 cm-1/K gives about 116 K from G; -5.15 / -0.034 gives about 151 K from 2D; the two agree within about 30%. Coefficients are for supported monolayer graphene measured between 83 and 373 K, so this is an extrapolation. The 2D shift per mW is non-linear: about -2.1 cm-1/mW between 0.5 and 2 mW and about -0.7 cm-1/mW between 2 and 5 mW.
observations.source: Calizo et al. 2007, arXiv 0708.1223, Table I p.7

observations.finding: Doping is excluded as the cause of the power dependence.
observations.evidence: Delta2D/DeltaG = 2.8 ± 0.2, whereas the hole-doping direction has slope 0.70. G broadens with power, while doping narrows G. The 2D/G height ratio is constant (G/2D height 0.366, 0.363, 0.372).
observations.source: Lee et al. 2012, Nat. Commun. 3, 1024 (arXiv 1209.0234, p.5); Das et al. 2008, Nat. Nanotechnol. 3, 210

observations.finding: Strain cannot be separated from heating by slope alone, but it is unlikely to be the cause.
observations.evidence: The strain slope 2.2 ± 0.2 is close to the observed 2.8 ± 0.2, and the heating slope is about 2.1 from Calizo. A static strain would not change reproducibly with laser power, and no G+/G- splitting is seen. Substrate thermal-expansion strain is part of the heating response.
observations.source: Lee 2012, Fig. 2; Ferrari and Basko 2013, Nat. Nanotechnol. 8, 235, p.20

observations.finding: At 0.5 mW the sample is near-neutral and nearly strain-free (qualitative, 532 nm).
observations.evidence: G 1581.14 cm-1 is within 0.5 cm-1 of the Lee origin 1581.6; 2D 2669.3 cm-1 is near the origin shifted to 532 nm (2676.9 minus about 8, from about 100 cm-1/eV dispersion, which is uncertain by about 3 cm-1). FWHM(G) 13.4 cm-1 is the low-doping value.
observations.source: Lee 2012 p.4; Ferrari and Basko 2013 p.7; Cancado 2011 Nano Lett. 11, 3190

observations.finding: Low defect density and monolayer-like 2D.
observations.evidence: No D peak above baseline (1300 to 1400 cm-1 maximum is at baseline level in all spectra). 2D is one Lorentzian of FWHM 26 cm-1, consistent with 1L on SiO2 (above 22 cm-1) and far narrower than turbostratic (about 50 cm-1). 2D/G height ratio is 2.7, below 4, which is not discriminating without the SiO2 thickness.
observations.source: Ferrari 2006, PRL 97, 187401 p.2-3; Neumann 2015, Nat. Commun. 6, 8429, Fig. 1h; Yoon 2009, PRB 80, 125422

caveats: The shift errors are fit statistics only; add about 0.2 to 0.3 cm-1 for calibration. The conclusions hold at that level.

The Lee 2012 strain/doping decomposition is validated only at 513 to 516 nm, for hole doping. At 532 nm the 2D reference position is shifted by an approximate dispersion (about 100 cm-1/eV), so the near-neutral, nearly strain-free statement is qualitative.

Thermal coefficients from Calizo 2007 are for 83 to 373 K on a particular substrate. Extrapolating to the temperatures reached here, and treating G and 2D separately, gives only an estimate of 115 to 150 K.

The 2D shift is sublinear in power, so a simple linear extrapolation to zero power is unreliable. Even 0.5 mW is probably somewhat heated, so the 0.5 mW positions are upper bounds for the cold G and 2D.
The spectra were taken in increasing power order. Irreversible laser-induced desorption, annealing or doping changes cannot be excluded without a repeat at 0.5 mW.

The 5 mW spectrum has a marginal feature near 2318 cm-1 (FWHM 33 ± 14, position error ±4), not interpreted. The fit also reports a broad background centred near 2554 cm-1 (FWHM 535), probably luminescence or background.
The 2D/G ratio of 2.7 is below 4, which is not discriminating without the SiO2 thickness (interference changes it by hundreds of percent). A small doping contribution is not excluded.
The area/power increase of about 12% with power is unexplained (focus, coupling or thermal change).
questions_for_user: Was a 0.5 mW spectrum retaken after the 5 mW exposure? If it matches the first, the changes were reversible heating and not laser-induced desorption, annealing or doping.
What is the SiO2 thickness? It sets the expected 2D/G intensity ratio (Yoon 2009), and the observed 2.7 is below the textbook 4.
Is the stated power measured at the sample, and what is the spot size? This is needed to scale heating.
What are the exfoliation and anneal history and the environment (air or vacuum)? They bear on the doping origin and on what the laser does to the surface.
What are the spectral resolution and calibration practice? Si FWHM is about 3.4 cm-1, but I assumed a calibration uncertainty of 0.2 to 0.3 cm-1.

limits: No quantitative strain or doping values are given. The G-2D vector relation is not valid at 532 nm, and heating contaminates all three spectra.
The data cannot give the true graphene temperature, the cold (zero-power) G and 2D positions, or the sign of any residual doping.
Static strain cannot be distinguished from thermal-expansion strain from the shifts alone; polarization-resolved G, a second laser, or a power series extrapolated to zero would be needed.
Data start at 450 cm-1, so the low-frequency shear modes (relevant for bilayer) are not observable. Layer number rests on the 2D line shape and width only.
Second-order and combination bands (such as LO+ZO') were not analysed; the analysis covers G, 2D, D and Si only.
